Albert Michelson's Harmonic Analyzer

A visual tour of a nineteenth-century machine that performs Fourier analysis. I photographed and designed the book.

My role
Photography and book design. Co-author with Bill Hammack and Bruce Carpenter.
With
Bill Hammack, Bruce Carpenter · Articulate Noise Books
Year
2014
Place
Urbana, Illinois
Format
Hardcover and paperback, 66 spreads, full color. Companion to a four-part EngineerGuy video series.
Links
Read the full book (PDF, 44 MB, engineerguy.com)Video series, part 1: IntroductionPart 2: SynthesisPart 3: AnalysisPart 4: Operation

It was no surprise that Bill, Bruce and I, a couple of academic engineers and a mathematician, were ecstatic to operate and analyze a machine that can calculate a Fourier transform by the turn of a crank. Along with a series of videos, we made a book to memorialize the design of one of physics' greatest minds.

I photographed the machine part by part against black and designed the book around those photographs: a spread for each of twenty parts, then the output it produces, Michelson's original 1898 paper, the math, and eight views of the whole machine.

Design

The machine does the work. Every part gets its own spread with a short text and a locator photo on the left and the part at full bleed on the right, so you can read the book as an explanation or just look at it.

Crank

Each part of the machine gets a spread. Text and a small locator photo on the left, the part at full bleed on the right.

Measuring stick

The parts are labeled on the machine itself, so the photographs double as diagrams.

Amplitude bars · Gears

Detail spreads, four frames to a page.

Introduction

Bill with the analyzer. The book opens with what the machine does before showing how.

Contents

Twenty parts, then output, Michelson's 1898 paper, the math, and eight views of the whole machine.
